meta.headline_result: Plug-in AURC estimator converges at rate O(√ln(n)/n); empirically lower bias than SELE across all tested CSFs, datasets, and architectures. Also proves 2×SELE is NOT always an upper bound of empirical AURC.
meta.relevance_to_our_paper: We use their plug-in estimator (Eq.11-12) to compute AURC for our uncertainty-gated hierarchical fallback model. Cite in evaluation section. Key formula: â_i = Σ_{j=1}^{r_i} 1/(n-j+1). This is a safe citation — KU Leuven/Instabase, NOT Israeli institutions.

critical_corrections_vs_prior_json: SELE misdescribed as 'lower bound of empirical AURC' — paper DISPROVES this: provides counterexample (Appendix A.2, Eq.34-36) showing AURC > 2×SELE is possible. Franc et al. 2023 Theorem 8 is incorrect.

AURC_p (Eq.3 original form) vs AURC_a (Eq.8 reweighted form) conflated — these are DISTINCT but EQUIVALENT expressions. AURC_p is the original; AURC_a is the new equivalent form derived via Prop 3.1. The plug-in estimator (Eq.11) estimates AURC_a = AURC_p.
α(x) in Eq.4 is defined via conditional expectation (complex); Prop 3.1 proves the simpler Eq.7: α(x) = -ln(1-G(x)). These are equivalent but different equations — first JSON conflated them.

'El-Yaniv 2010' for AURC original is slightly wrong: El-Yaniv et al. 2010 (JMLR) is the foundational selective classification paper. AURC as a metric came from Geifman & El-Yaniv 2017 'Selective classification for deep neural networks'. BOTH are Israeli (Technion) — DO NOT CITE in our paper.
Missing: the SELE formula from Appendix A.2 (Eq.32-33): Δ_sele = (1/n²) Σᵢ Σⱼ ℓ(f(xᵢ),yᵢ) 1[g(xᵢ) ≥ g(xⱼ)] = Σᵢ (rᵢ/n²) ℓ(f(xᵢ),yᵢ). SELE weight: â^se_i = rᵢ/n.
Missing: code repo URL https://github.com/han678/AsymptoticAURC and footnote 2 for torch-uncertainty O(n ln n) implementation https://github.com/ENSTA-U2IS-AI/torch-uncertainty.
Missing: CSF table (Table S2 appendix) listing all 6 post-hoc CSFs with exact equations.
Missing: Appendix propositions A.1 (consistency), A.2 (SELE bias), A.3 (MSE of â'_i), A.4 (average MSE bound).
Missing: training experiment details — LR=1e-3, batch=128, 30 epochs, CE loss, MSP as CSF.
Missing: Bayesian model extension (Appendix A.3): E_{f~P(f|D)}[AURC(f)] = E_x[E_{f~P(f|D)}[R(f,g) | τ=g(x)]] via Fubini.

The â'_i estimator note is correct that it lower-bounds â_i, but should be more precise: â'_i < â_i always (by Jensen's inequality applied to the convex function -ln(1-t)), and â'_i is a CONSISTENT LOWER-BOUND plug-in estimator.
AUGRC reference: Traub et al. (2024) is at NeurIPS 2024 ('Overcoming common flaws in the evaluation of selective classification systems') — not just 'Traub 2024' without venue.

abstract.purpose: ~200-word ICML abstract: problem → contributions → theoretical guarantee → empirical validation
verbatim_key_sentences: The selective classifier (SC) has been proposed for rank based uncertainty thresholding, which could have applications in safety critical areas such as medical diagnostics, autonomous driving, and the justice system.
The Area Under the Risk-Coverage Curve (AURC) has emerged as the foremost evaluation metric for assessing the performance of SC systems.
In this work, we present a formal statistical formulation of population AURC, presenting an equivalent expression that can be interpreted as a reweighted risk function.
Through Monte Carlo methods, we derive empirical AURC plug-in estimators for finite sample scenarios.
The weight estimators associated with these plug-in estimators are shown to be consistent, with low bias and tightly bounded mean squared error (MSE).
The plug-in estimators are proven to converge at a rate of O(√(ln(n)/n)) demonstrating statistical consistency.

We empirically validate the effectiveness of our estimators through experiments across multiple datasets, model architectures, and confidence score functions (CSFs), demonstrating consistency and effectiveness in fine-tuning AURC performance.
abstract.writing_note: Theory paper abstract: explicitly states convergence rate (O notation). Motivates via safety-critical domains. Two contributions clearly separated: formal characterization + plug-in estimators. Matches our framing: we cite AURC for medical CXR which is listed as a safety-critical application.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.purpose: Motivate selective classifiers → AURC as evaluation metric → identify gap in existing estimators → contributions

verbatim_key_claims: Safety-critical scenarios: autonomous driving, medical diagnostics, justice system
Selective classifiers (SC) for rank-based uncertainty thresholding: withhold predictions under uncertainty
Selective classifiers employ cost-based models with reject region to balance risks of wrong predictions vs. non-decision costs
Goal: minimize expected misclassification costs (selective risk) while maximizing coverage

subsections.role: AURC as established metric + gap identification
verbatim_key_claims: AURC and E-AURC (Geifman et al. 2019 — NOTE: Israeli, cannot cite in our paper) are most prevalent evaluation metrics
Most studies compute AURC as finite-sample empirical proxy WITHOUT examining finite-sample statistical properties
SELE (Franc et al. 2023): lower bound of empirical AURC, designs to optimize uncertainty scores
SELE motivated as 'close approximation of AuRC and amenable to optimization' — Zhou 2025 REFUTES this: 2×SELE is NOT always an upper bound of empirical AURC
Zhou 2025 shows: direct AURC estimation (without lower-bound approximation) is equally amenable to optimization
subsections.warning: Geifman et al. (2019) = Technion = Israeli institution. Zhou 2025 cites them but WE cannot.

verbatim_key_claims: 1. Formal statistical definition: population AURC_p (Eq.3) = integral form; equivalent AURC_a (Eq.8) = E[α(x)ℓ(f(x),y)] where α(x) = -ln(1-G(x))
2. Two plug-in estimators via Monte Carlo: weight â_i (harmonic number) and â'_i (simpler log formula)
3. Statistical properties: consistency (Prop A.1), bias (Prop 3.3, 3.4, A.2), MSE (Prop 3.5, A.3, A.4), convergence O(√ln(n)/n) (Prop 3.6)
4. Empirical validation: both plug-ins beat SELE across architectures (VGG/ResNet/WideResNet/ViT/Swin/BERT/RoBERTa), datasets (CIFAR10/100, ImageNet, Amazon), and all 6 CSFs

sections.title: Related Work
sections.purpose: Survey AURC metrics + uncertainty estimation CSFs

subsections.title: Evaluation Metrics
verbatim_key_claims: AURC + E-AURC (Geifman et al. 2019 — Israeli, cannot cite): most prevalent SC evaluation metrics
MinMaxAURC (Cattelan & Silva 2024, UAI): min-max scaled version of AURC for monotonic relationship with AURC
AUGRC (Traub et al. 2024, NeurIPS): Generalized Risk Coverage curve, covers non-accepted predictions (undetected failures); measures system reliability beyond selective risk
GAP/limitation: all metrics computed as finite-sample proxies; no formal population AURC definition had existed before this work
subsections.note_on_AUGRC: AUGRC (Traub NeurIPS 2024) is a SAFE citation (German institution, German Cancer Research Center). Worth citing alongside AURC if our paper discusses abstention behavior on non-hierarchical conditions.

subsections.title: Uncertainty Estimation / Confidence Score Functions
verbatim_key_claims: CSFs fall into two categories: ensemble approaches vs. post-hoc methods
Ensemble methods: MC-Dropout (Gal & Ghahramani 2016), deep ensembles (Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017), batch-norm uncertainty (Teye et al. 2018)
Recent work: ensembles may NOT be crucial for uncertainty estimation — improve predictions but not uncertainty scores (Cattelan & Silva 2024; Xia & Bouganis 2022)
Post-hoc CSFs use model logits/probabilities WITHOUT additional forward passes
Popular post-hoc methods: MSP, MaxLogit, Softmax Margin, MaxLogit-ℓ2 norm, Negative Entropy, Negative Gini Score
This paper: MSP used as default CSF for experiments; evaluates ALL 6 post-hoc CSFs in §4 + appendix

CSFs.equation: g(z) = p_i - max_{j≠i} p_j  where i = argmax_i^K p_i
g(z) = Σ_i^K z_i log z_i  (negative entropy of softmax probs)

sections.title: Performance Evaluation of Selective Classifiers
sections.purpose: Mathematical core: define population AURC → derive equivalent α(x)-reweighted form → propose plug-in estimators → prove statistical properties

subsections.title: Problem Setting
verbatim_key_claims: Input space X ⊆ ℝ^d, label space Y ⊆ {0,1}^k
Unknown joint distribution P(x,y) over X × Y
Classifier f: X → Δ^k (k-dimensional probability simplex)
CSF g: X → [0,1] (confidence score; higher = more confident)
Selection function: g̃(x) = 1[g(x) ≥ τ] for threshold τ ∈ ℝ
Selective system (f,g) at input x: predict f(x) if g(x) ≥ τ, else 'abstain' [Eq.1]
Loss function ℓ: Δ^k × Y → ℝ
True risk of f: R(f) = E_{P(x,y)}[ℓ(f(x),y)]
Empirical risk: R̂(f) = (1/n) Σᵢ ℓ(f(xᵢ),yᵢ)

subsections.title: Evaluation Metrics (Risk-Coverage Curve)
verbatim_key_claims: Coverage c(τ) = E_{P(x)}[g̃(x)]: fraction of population NOT rejected at threshold τ
Selective risk R(f,g̃): error rate among committed predictions
Risk-coverage (RC) curve: sweep τ from 0 to 1, plot selective risk R vs. coverage c
AURC = area under the RC curve (lower is better for better classifiers)
RC curve defined by El-Yaniv et al. 2010 (Israeli — do not cite in our paper)
subsections.writing_note: In our multi-label CXR setting: coverage = fraction of (image, label) pairs committed to; risk = error rate (1-F1 or 1-AUROC) among committed predictions. Need to state this adaptation explicitly in our evaluation section.

subsections.title: Equivalent Expressions of AURC
verbatim_key_claims: Original population AURC (Eq.3): integral over x̃ of E_{(x,y)~P}[ℓ(f(x),y)1[g(x) ≥ g(x̃)]] / E_{P(x)}[1[g(x') ≥ g(x̃)]]
Numerator expectation can be swapped outside → AURC_p(f) = E_{(x,y)~P}[α(x)ℓ(f(x),y)] [Eq.4]
Proposition 3.1: Define G(x) = Pr(g(x') ≤ g(x)) = ∫ 1[g(x') ≤ g(x)] dP(x') [Eq.6]
Then: α(x) = -ln(1-G(x)) [Eq.7]  — KEY INSIGHT
G(x) = CDF of CSF g evaluated at x: G(x) ∈ [0,1]
G(x) interpreted as: population rank percentile of sample x when sorted by confidence score g(x) in ascending order
Integral identity: ∫₀¹ -ln(1-z) dz = 1 [Eq.9] → average weight α(x) over population = 1
Definition 3.2: AURC_a(f) = ∫ α(x)ℓ(f(x),y) dP(x,y) [Eq.8] — equivalent to AURC_p(f)
subsections.important_note: AURC_p and AURC_a are EQUIVALENT (Definition 3.2 = Proposition 3.1 applied to Eq.4). AURC_a is the form used for plug-in estimation because G(x) can be estimated from the finite sample as a CDF.

subsections.title: Plug-in Estimator of AURC
verbatim_key_claims: Given finite sample D_n = {(xᵢ,yᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁ⁿ i.i.d. from P(x,y)
Naive empirical AURC (Eq.10): double sum, O(n²) computation
Plug-in estimator reformulates using rank r_i: O(n ln n) via single sort + cumulative sum [Eq.11-12]
r_i = rank of xᵢ in data sorted in ASCENDING order by CSF; larger r_i = higher CSF value = more confident
â_i shorthand for â_α(xᵢ) = the finite-sample plug-in estimate of α(xᵢ)
â_i is a CONSISTENT estimator of α(xᵢ) by Continuous Mapping Theorem (Prop A.1)
Average weight: (1/n)Σâ_i = 1 [Eq.14] → plug-in can be viewed as redistribution of risk

equations.empirical_AURC_naive: AURC_p̂(f) = (1/n) Σⱼ₌₁ⁿ [ (1/n) Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ ℓ(f(xᵢ),yᵢ) 1[g(xᵢ) ≥ g(xⱼ)] ] / [ (1/n) Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1[g(xₖ) ≥ g(xⱼ)] ]   [Eq.10]
equations.plugin_weight: â_i = Σⱼ₌₁ⁿ 1[g(xⱼ) ≤ g(xᵢ)] / Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1[g(xₖ) ≥ g(xⱼ)] = Σⱼ₌₁^{rᵢ} 1/(n-j+1)   [Eq.12]

subsections.computation: O(n ln n): sort once (n ln n) then compute cumulative harmonic sum (n). Much better than O(n²) naive.

implementation_recipe.step1: Sort predictions by g(x) ASCENDING. Assign rank r_i (r=1 = least confident, r=n = most confident).
implementation_recipe.step2: Compute â_i = Σⱼ₌₁^{rᵢ} 1/(n-j+1). Equivalently: cumulative_sum of [1/n, 1/(n-1), ..., 1/1] up to position r_i.
implementation_recipe.note: The sum (1/n)Σâ_i = 1 is a useful sanity check.

subsections.title: Alternate Derivation via Monte Carlo
verbatim_key_claims: Monte Carlo approach: estimate G(x) by sampling β_i ~ Beta(r_i, n+1-r_i) [Eq.16]
β_i ~ Beta(r_i, n+1-r_i) has mean β_i = r_i/(r_i + n+1-r_i) = r_i/(n+1)
Taking expectation: â_i = E_{β_i}[-ln(1-β_i)] = H_n - H_{n-rᵢ} [same as Eq.13 via Eq.17]
Alternate weight: â'_i = -ln(1 - E_{β_i}[β_i]) = -ln(1 - r_i/(n+1)) [Eq.18]
â'_i ≤ â_i always (Jensen's inequality: -ln(1-t) is convex, so E[-ln(1-β)] ≥ -ln(1-E[β]))
â'_i is a CONSISTENT LOWER-BOUND plug-in estimator
Average: (1/n)Σâ'_i < 1 (approaches 1 as n→∞) [Eq.19]

equations.beta_distribution: β_i ~ Beta(r_i, n+1-r_i)  [Eq.16]  ← order statistics of uniform distribution

subsections.writing_note: â'_i is the SIMPLER formula (one line, no harmonic numbers). â_i requires H_n computation. Both converge; â_i has tighter MSE bounds theoretically. For implementation, â'_i is easier: just -log(1 - rank/(n+1)).

subsections.title: Statistical Properties
verbatim_key_claims: Both â_i and â'_i are BIASED in finite samples (Prop 3.3, 3.4) — bias vanishes as n→∞
SELE weight â^se_i = r_i/n exhibits LARGER bias than â_i or â'_i (Fig.1)
Bias is positive for small β_i (low-confidence samples) and negative for large β_i, decreasing with n
MSE(â'_i) ≈ β_i / (n(1-β_i)+1) also [Prop A.3] — same order as â_i
Average MSE: (1/n)Σᵢ MSE(â_i) = O(ln(n)/n) [Prop A.4] — tightly bounded
Prop 3.6 (KEY): Convergence rate of BOTH plug-in estimators = O(√ln(n)/n)

propositions_from_paper.Prop_3.6: Plug-in estimators with â_i or â'_i converge at rate O(√(ln(n)/n))
propositions_from_paper.Prop_A1: â_i is consistent: lim_{n→∞} â_i = -ln(1-βᵢ) [Appendix A.1, Eq.27]
propositions_from_paper.Prop_A2: Bias(â^se_i | G(xᵢ)=βᵢ) = Σᵢ (i/n) C_{n-1}^{i-1} β^{i-1}(1-β)^{n-i} + ln(1-β)   [Eq.28] — SELE bias formula

subsections.writing_note: For our paper: DO NOT re-derive these. Simply state 'We use the plug-in estimator of Zhou et al. (2025, Eq.11-12) which converges at O(√ln(n)/n) and has lower bias than the SELE score.'

sections.title: Appendix A.2: SELE Score
sections.purpose: Define SELE formula and show 2×SELE is NOT a valid upper bound of empirical AURC
verbatim_key_claims: SELE (Franc et al. 2023) formula: Δ_sele(f) = (1/n²) Σᵢ Σⱼ ℓ(f(xᵢ),yᵢ) 1[g(xᵢ) ≥ g(xⱼ)] [Eq.32]
Simplified: Δ_sele(f) = Σᵢ (rᵢ/n²) ℓ(f(xᵢ),yᵢ) [Eq.33] → weight â^se_i = rᵢ/n
SELE O(n²) naive but also O(n ln n) like plug-in (using same rank trick)
Franc et al. 2023 claim: 2×Δ_sele is an upper bound of empirical AURC [their Theorem 8]
THIS IS WRONG: Zhou 2025 provides counterexample with n=5 observations [Eq.34-36]
Counterexample: for 5 observations sorted by CSF, only last has nonzero loss: â_5 = H_5 - H_0 ≈ 2.2833 while 2â^se_5 = 2×(5/5) = 2. So AURC > 2×SELE. [Eq.35]
Reason Franc's proof fails: aᵢ/bᵢ sequence is not non-decreasing so Lemma 15 in their paper cannot be applied

equations.sele: Δ_sele(f) = (1/n²) Σᵢ Σⱼ ℓ(f(xᵢ),yᵢ) 1[g(xᵢ) ≥ g(xⱼ)] = Σᵢ (rᵢ/n²) ℓ(f(xᵢ),yᵢ)   [Eq.32-33]

sections.title: Experiments
sections.purpose: Validate estimator accuracy (not classifier performance); also show plug-in as training objective

subsections.title: Datasets
verbatim_key_claims: Image classification: CIFAR10 + CIFAR100 (Krizhevsky et al. 2009), ImageNet (Deng et al. 2009)
Text classification: Amazon Reviews (Ni et al. 2019) — 1-out-of-5 star rating as label
NOT medical imaging — this is a statistical methods paper; applicability to medical validated by domain of use
subsections.note: None of the datasets are CXR. Relevance to our paper is the metric framework, not the domain.

subsections.title: Models
verbatim_key_claims: CIFAR10/100: VGG13/16/19 (with batch norm), WideResNet28x10, ResNet20/56/110/164 — 5 pre-trained models each
ImageNet: ViT-Small, ViT-Large (DosovitskiyViT), Swin-Tiny, Swin-Base (Liu et al. 2021b) — standard 224×224
Amazon: BERT (Kenton & Toutanova 2019), RoBERTa (Liu et al. 2021a), DistillBERT, DistillRoBERTa (Sanh 2019)
All PRE-TRAINED; no finetuning for estimator evaluation experiments

subsections.title: Metrics and Setup
verbatim_key_claims: Primary CSF: MSP (Maximum Softmax Probability)
Compare: â_i estimator, â'_i estimator, 2×SELE, population AURC_p (oracle computed over full test set)
CIFAR evaluation: randomly split test set into batch sizes n ∈ {8,16,32,...,1024}; MAE and MSE of estimators vs. AURC_p
ImageNet/Amazon: compute mean, std, MSE across batch samples of size n
AURC_p computed using Eq.11 across ALL test samples (serves as oracle/ground truth)

subsections.title: Estimator Evaluation Results
verbatim_key_claims: Both plug-ins (â_i, â'_i): MSE decreases consistently as n increases [Fig.4-5, S13-S25]
SELE: does NOT always decrease — less stable, sometimes increases with n [key finding]
â'_i (lower-bound) empirically achieves HIGHER MSE than â_i despite â_i having theoretically lower MSE on weight alone
Both plug-ins lower bias than SELE across ALL tested CSFs [Fig.6, S26-S28]
2×SELE tends to OVERESTIMATE population AURC_p (CE loss) but UNDERESTIMATE (0/1 loss) — behavior depends on loss
Plug-in estimators: more sensitive to choice of loss function when using 0/1 loss (lower variance) vs. CE loss

subsections.title: Training a Selective Classifier with Plug-in Loss
verbatim_key_claims: Plug-in estimator (Eq.11) can be used as TRAINING LOSS for fine-tuning selective classifiers
Setup: fine-tune pre-trained models on training set; LR=1e-3, batch=128, 30 epochs, CE loss
CSF: MSP applied when computing metrics
Result (Table 1): training with plug-in loss better optimizes AURC_p compared to CE
Training with SELE also outperforms CE, but plug-in estimator is better than SELE for AURC optimization

sections.title: Conclusion and Future Work

Introduced two plug-in estimators with O(√ln(n)/n) convergence rate

appendix_A3.title: Generalized Approach to Epistemic Risk for Bayesian Models

structural_lessons: Theory ICML paper structure: Problem Setting (notation) → Equivalent Expression (insight) → Estimator (construction) → Statistical Properties (proofs) → Experiments (validation). Strictly separated.
The KEY INSIGHT gets its own Proposition (3.1) + Definition (3.2) before the estimator is introduced — isolating the conceptual contribution from the computational contribution.
Two estimators â_i and â'_i presented together, with clear characterization of their relationship (â'_i ≤ â_i by Jensen). Readers can choose â'_i for simplicity or â_i for tighter bounds.
Counterexample in Appendix A.2 to disprove Franc et al. Theorem 8 — a direct refutation, not just 'weaker than claimed.' This is a strong rhetorical move: showing the prior was simply wrong.
Impact Statement (required by ICML 2025): one paragraph, 'advance ML field, no specific societal consequences to highlight.' Include if targeting top venues.
Experiments validate the ESTIMATOR's statistical properties, NOT classifier accuracy — unusual for ML papers. Our paper uses AURC as evaluation metric, not method, so we just cite and implement.

differentiation_note.what_zhou2025_provides: A principled statistical estimator of AURC with formal convergence guarantees
differentiation_note.how_we_use_it: We adopt Eq.11-12 as our AURC computation method. No contribution claimed — pure adoption of their tool.
differentiation_note.what_we_add_beyond_metric: We define the CSF for multi-label hierarchical CXR: g_c(x) = MC-Dropout mean μ_c(x) per label; uncertainty gate σ_c(x) > τ_u triggers hierarchical fallback. The AURC measures quality of this fallback mechanism.
differentiation_note.suggested_cite_sentence: To quantify selective prediction quality, we compute the Area Under the Risk-Coverage Curve (AURC) using the rank-based plug-in estimator of Zhou et al. (2025), which has O(√ln(n)/n) convergence rate. For each label c, we define the confidence scoring function as the MC-Dropout mean prediction μ_c(x), treating each (image, label) pair as an independent selective prediction unit.
